sections.h: Chapters 1 to 3: what God has done
sections.b: The first half of the letter is praise and teaching. God has chosen, adopted, redeemed and sealed a people in Christ (1:3-14); has made them alive from death by grace through faith (2:1-10); has made Jews and Gentiles one new humanity and one temple (2:11-22); and has made this secret known through Paul (3:1-13). Two prayers (1:15-23; 3:14-21) ask that the readers know it. The first half ends in a doxology.
sections.refs: Ephesians 1:3-14; Ephesians 1:15-23; Ephesians 2:1-10; Ephesians 2:11-22; Ephesians 3:1-13; Ephesians 3:14-21

sections.h: Who wrote it, and to whom
sections.b: The opening names Paul (1:1; 3:1), but the authorship is disputed, and 'in Ephesus' is missing from some of the oldest manuscripts. The notes at 1:1, 1:15 and 3:2 and the book page weigh the readings: Paul himself, Paul through a co-worker, a follower after his death; written to Ephesus, or to churches of Asia Minor generally. Colossians (the Letter to the Colossians, written to a church near Laodicea) is close in wording to Ephesians, and the order of their writing is disputed.

common: Most scholars agree that chapters 1 to 3 are doctrine in the form of praise and prayer and that chapters 4 to 6 turn to conduct.
uncommon: Some hold that the letter is a single liturgy, an extended prayer from start to finish, with the instructions of 4 to 6 as its application.

sections.b: Ephesians is named for Ephesus, though some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words 'in Ephesus' (1:1). The city's setting fits the letter: the powers and magic of 1:21, 2:2, 3:10 and 6:12 were everyday realities in a city of Artemis, and Clinton Arnold has argued that the letter's picture of the powers makes best sense there. Paul lived in the city about three years (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31), which makes his 'I heard of your faith' (1:15) and 'if you have indeed heard' (3:2) puzzling.

In Ephesians Paul is 'the prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles' (3:1; 4:1), the least of the saints who was given grace to tell the Gentiles of the 'riches of Christ, riches no one can trace out' (3:8), and the steward of the mystery (3:2-9). Whether he wrote this himself or it was written in his name by a follower is disputed. In either case the letter keeps his image as the apostle to the Gentiles and a suffering servant.

God 'chose us in Christ before the world was founded, to be holy and without blame' and 'decided beforehand that we would be adopted as his children'. The verbs eklegomai and proorizo are at the center of the long debate about election and predestination. The card at Ephesians 1 gives the answers of the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Methodist and Baptist traditions. Notice that the stated aim of the choice is holiness, and that the passage is a hymn of praise, not an argument about who is excluded.

common: The choice is 'in Christ', which every tradition affirms.
uncommon: Some scholars read 1:4 as corporate: God chose the church as a people in Christ, and individuals are chosen by joining it.

sections.b: The only adoption text in Ephesians says God decided beforehand that believers would be adopted as his children through Jesus Christ, 'to belong to himself'. Like Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:5 it uses the Roman legal word for taking someone into a family with an heir's rights. In Ephesians, the adopted people are Jews and Gentiles together, and the next verses speak of redemption and inheritance (1:7, 11, 14).

Grace (charis) runs through the letter: 'the glory of his grace, which he freely gave us' (1:6), 'the wealth of his grace' (1:7), 'It is by grace that you have been saved' (2:5, 8), 'how very rich his grace is' (2:7), and the grace given to Paul (3:2, 7-8). In 2:8-9 grace is set against works as the cause of salvation, with faith as the way it is received. The card at 2:8-10 sets out how the churches have understood it.

Faith in Ephesians is the means by which grace is received: 'It is by grace that you have been saved, through faith' (2:8). Faith is also the way Christ settles in the readers' hearts (3:17). The expression 'through faith in him' in 3:12 raises the question whether the Greek means faith in Christ or his own faithfulness (compare Romans 3:22; Galatians 2:16). The Plain English Translation follows 'faith in him' and gives the other reading in the note.

common: Faith is the means and not the cause of salvation.
uncommon: Some scholars read 'through his faithfulness' in 3:12, taking Christ's own faithfulness as the ground of confidence.

sections.b: The unusual tense of Ephesians 2:5 and 2:8, 'you have been saved' (a perfect: done, with lasting results), puts salvation as a present possession. Elsewhere Paul speaks of salvation as still ahead (Romans 5:9-10; 13:11). Ephesians has both: 'saved' now (2:8), and the 'day of redemption' still to come (4:30; 1:14). The first half of the letter makes salvation a rescue from death, from the powers of this age and from alienation from God and from one another.
sections.refs: Ephesians 2:5; Ephesians 2:8; Ephesians 1:14; Ephesians 4:30; Romans 5:9-10; Romans 13:11

sections.b: The word 'justify' does not appear in Ephesians, but 2:8-10 is the New Testament passage most often joined to Romans 3 to teach justification by grace through faith and not by works. Reformation readers heard 'works' as any human effort to earn favor. The New Perspective (Sanders and later scholars) hears boundary markers of Jewish identity, which fits the context of 2:11-22. The card at Ephesians 2 gives the churches' teaching.

sections.h: Ephesians: the church as body, building and fullness
sections.b: Ephesians has more to say about the church than any other letter. It is Christ's body, and he is its head (1:22-23); one new humanity (2:15); a household, a building on a foundation of apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone, and a holy temple (2:19-22); the place where God's wisdom is made known to the powers (3:10); and the people who give God glory 'in the church and in Christ Jesus' (3:21). Chapters 4 and 5 add the body that grows (4:11-16) and the bride (5:25-32). The singular 'church' here means the whole people of God, not one congregation; this is one reason some scholars date the letter later.

sections.h: Ephesians: the mystery in four places
sections.b: Ephesians uses 'mystery' more than any other letter. In 1:9 it is God's will to gather everything in Christ; in 3:3-6 it is that Gentiles are heirs together with Israel; in 5:32 it is the great meaning of marriage in Genesis 2:24, applied to Christ and the church; in 6:19 it is the good news itself. These are different faces of one hidden purpose, now revealed. Paul says he was given the revelation and is its steward (3:2-3).

The plan 'to bring all things together in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth' is the only place Paul states God's goal as the unification of the whole creation. Ephesians 1:22 (Christ head over all things) and 4:10 (he fills all things) belong to the same picture. Irenaeus and the Eastern fathers built their teaching on it.

The letter's picture of Christ breaking down 'the middle wall, the wall that fenced us apart' gathers up the Temple barrier, the law as a fence and the hostility between Jews and Gentiles. See the notes at 2:14-16 and the card on 2:15.

Three passages in the first half speak of powers. Christ is 'far above every ruler, authority, power and lordship' (1:21). The readers once followed the 'ruler of the domain of the air' (2:2). And through the church God's wisdom is made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly world (3:10). The fourth passage, 6:12, is in the second half. Together they say that the powers are real, are created and are below Christ, and that the church's life is a witness to them.

common: Most readers take the powers as spiritual beings.
uncommon: Some also see human structures such as empires, laws and economies in the same terms.

sections.h: Ephesians 1:13-14: the seal and down payment
sections.b: The Spirit is the seal (a mark of ownership) and the down payment (a first installment of the promised inheritance) given to believers who have heard and believed. Paul returns to the seal in 4:30. The Spirit also gives 'a spirit of wisdom and revelation' (1:17, if that is the Holy Spirit), 'access' to the Father (2:18), the building of the temple (2:22) and strength in the inner self (3:16). Churches differ on when the sealing happens; see the card at 1:13.
sections.refs: Ephesians 1:13-14; Ephesians 1:17; Ephesians 2:18; Ephesians 2:22; Ephesians 3:16; Ephesians 4:30

sections.b: Christ's exaltation is told in the language of Psalm 110:1 and Psalm 8:6: God 'raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly world, far above every ruler, authority, power and lordship'. Believers are raised and seated with him (2:6). The ascension is also the subject of 4:8-10, in the second part of this book.

The church is a building 'on the apostles and prophets as the foundation, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone'. The image draws on Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22, and it is joined to the temple picture of 2:21-22. A few readers hold that the Greek akrogoniaios means the capstone at the top, not the corner at the base.

sections.h: Ephesians 2:21-22: the church as holy temple
sections.b: 'The whole building is fitted together, and it is growing up as a temple that is holy in the Lord... a home for God in the Spirit.' The community, not a place, is where God now lives. For the readers in Ephesus, the image would compare with the temple of Artemis, and for Jewish believers it would recall the barrier of the Temple in Jerusalem (2:14).

Believers are 'what he has made, created in Christ Jesus to do good works' (2:10), and Christ creates 'in him one new humanity out of the two' (2:15). The language is of creation, not repair. Chapter 4 adds the 'new self, created according to God' (4:24) in the second part of this book.

'By nature we were children of anger, like everyone else.' The Plain English Translation's word for orge is 'anger'. Paul does not describe God's anger here, only the readers' condition under it before Christ. The verse has been used for original sin; see the note.

sections.h: Ephesians 3:19: filled with all the fullness of God
sections.b: Paul prays that the readers 'be filled up to all the fullness of God'. Some readers hear in the phrase the language of sharing in God's own life (compare 2 Peter 1:4). Together with 1:23 (the church as the fullness of Christ) and 4:13 (the full measure of Christ), it speaks of being filled with God's own fullness. Catholic teaching speaks of divinization in general (Catechism 460, whose note names Athanasius and Aquinas).

sections.h: Ephesians: 'to the praise of his glory'
sections.b: The refrain of the great blessing is 'to the praise of his glory' (1:6, 12, 14). It names the aim of God's whole work. The letter also speaks of 'the wealth of the glory' of God's inheritance (1:18), of the Father of glory (1:17), and of the readers' glory in Paul's sufferings (3:13). It ends the first half with 'to him belongs the glory, in the church and in Christ Jesus' (3:21).
sections.refs: Ephesians 1:6; Ephesians 1:12; Ephesians 1:14; Ephesians 1:17-18; Ephesians 3:13; Ephesians 3:21

sections.b: Paul reports two prayers for the readers. The first (1:15-23) asks that they know God, his hope, his inheritance and his power. The second (3:14-19) asks for strength, the presence of Christ in the heart, rooted love, and a knowledge of Christ's love that goes beyond knowing. Both are addressed to the Father, and both are asking for understanding. A blessing (1:3-14) and a doxology (3:20-21) frame them.

The church is built on 'the apostles and prophets' as its foundation (2:20), and the mystery was revealed to 'his holy apostles and prophets' (3:5). Most readers take 'prophets' as New Testament prophets. The question whether the offices continue today divides the churches; see the card at 2:20 and the note at 4:11 in the second part.

Gentiles were 'cut off from the commonwealth of Israel and were strangers to the covenants of the promise' (2:12). Now they are 'citizens together with the saints' (2:19), and they are 'heirs together, members of the body together, and sharers together in the promise' (3:6). Whether this makes the church a new Israel, a widened Israel or a people distinct from Israel is the question on the card at 3:6.

sections.h: Ephesians 2:11: the circumcision and the uncircumcision
sections.b: The letter recalls the old labels, 'the circumcision' and 'the uncircumcision', with a note that the first is only 'made in the flesh by human hands'. Circumcision is the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:9-14), and in Paul's day it was the main marker between Jew and Gentile. Paul does not say it was wrong; he says it no longer divides.

Christ 'put out of effect the law of commandments with its rules' to make one new humanity. This is one of the most disputed sentences in Paul on the law. The card at 2:15 sets out the churches' readings: the whole law, its ceremonial part, its barrier function, its condemnation, or its role in Gentile exclusion.

The Gentiles 'were strangers to the covenants' (2:12) and are 'no longer strangers and resident aliens' (2:19). The Old Testament had its own foreigners and sojourners (Leviticus 19:33-34), who were to be treated like citizens. Ephesians takes the image and applies it to the church's welcome of those who were outsiders.

Christ himself 'came with the good news of peace' (2:17), and the Gentiles are heirs 'through the good news' (3:6). Paul is its servant (3:7), and his task is to tell the Gentiles the good news of the riches of Christ (3:8).

sections.h: Ephesians 2:18 and 1:3-14: Father, Son and Spirit
sections.b: No passage in Ephesians states the Trinity as doctrine, but the three persons are named together again and again: in the blessing (the Father who chooses, the Son who redeems, the Spirit who seals, 1:3-14), in 2:18 ('through him... in one Spirit... to the Father'), in 2:22 and in the prayer of 3:14-17. Later writers on the Trinity cite the letter often.

The readers' former condition is described as death in trespasses and sins, a walk after the age of this world and its ruler, and a life in the desires of the flesh as 'children of anger' (2:1-3). The passage has been cited for the doctrine of inherited sin, but Paul's point is the readers' common condition before Christ. See the note at 2:3.
